entries.claim: Close to half of store visitors look only at the first two screenshots.

facts.of: look only at first two screenshots

entries.appliesWhen: Store visitors browsing a listing; SplitMetrics 2024 sample of about 200 apps and 3,500+ tests across both stores (category mix not stated).

support.excerpt: AppFollow, quoting SplitMetrics 2024: 'close to half of store visitors look only at the first two screenshots'; 'just 7% reach the fifth'.

entries.useFor: Justify putting the whole pitch into screenshots 1-2 of the Rogue Legend set; do not quote as Google Play data.
entries.researcherNote: Single origin (SplitMetrics report is gated, so the figure is second-hand via AppFollow). Not split by store, game genre or country; no Google Play-specific scroll data was found anywhere.

entries.claim: Fewer than one in five App Store visitors scroll through a full five-screenshot gallery.
entries.appliesWhen: App Store galleries of five screenshots; SplitMetrics 2018 (1,800 tests) and AppAgent 2017 (five apps, 25,000+ visitors).

support.excerpt: SplitMetrics 2018: only 11% scroll through all 5 portrait images and 15% through all 5 landscape images.
AppAgent 2017: only 9% scroll portrait screenshots, 17% for gamers, 5% for landscape.

entries.useFor: Assume most visitors never see screenshots 4-8; put the strongest hook and the core loop early.
entries.researcherNote: Both data sets are old (2017-18), iOS-era layouts; the two disagree on which orientation is scrolled more (see the orientation entries). No comparable Google Play scroll-depth study was found.

entries.claim: About 60% of app store visitors are 'decisive' (decide without engaging with the gallery) and about 40% are 'explorers'.
entries.appliesWhen: Storemaven's visitor model, derived from its own testing platform (undated, 'over one billion data points').

support.excerpt: Storemaven guest post: 'Decisive Visitors represents 60% of all app store traffic'; the remaining 40% are explorers.

entries.useFor: Framing only: design the first-impression frame for people who will never scroll.
entries.researcherNote: Vendor-only, undated, method not published; storemaven.com itself is no longer fetchable.

entries.claim: Explorer visitors show 5-15% higher day-2 retention than instant installers.
entries.appliesWhen: Storemaven audience model; App Store and Google Play not distinguished.

support.excerpt: Storemaven: explorers show 'second day retention 5-15% above instant installers' and higher conversion to paying users.

entries.useFor: Optional argument that a richer gallery attracts higher-quality players; do not overweight.
entries.researcherNote: Vendor-only, undated, no method.

entries.claim: Store visitors decide within seconds: about 7 seconds on the listing on average, and about half decide on first impression.
entries.appliesWhen: AppAgent 2017 (five apps) and Storemaven (via Apptamin/Mobilespoon).

support.excerpt: AppAgent 2017: users spend an average of just 7 seconds on the store listing page.
Apptamin quoting Storemaven: '50% of all installers make a decision only based on your first impression'.

entries.useFor: Design for glance value; test at thumbnail size.
entries.researcherNote: Two vendor sources, small or undocumented samples, old.

entries.claim: Screenshot 1 should communicate the core promise on its own, like a stand-alone ad.
entries.appliesWhen: Any listing where users see only the first frame(s); advice, not a measured effect.

support.excerpt: Apple: the first one to three images appear in App Store search results, 'so make sure these highlight the essence of your app'.
AppFollow: frame one communicates the core promise; frames two and three reinforce value through use cases or outcomes.
SEM Nexus: 'treat screenshot 1 as a standalone ad unit, not a gallery opener' (self-described working hypothesis, not a controlled study).
AppScreenshotStudio: panoramic sets work only when the first frame stands alone as a complete selling point.

entries.useFor: Make screenshot 1 for Rogue Legend a complete pitch (genre + hook + character) without needing frame 2.
entries.researcherNote: Convergent advice from four origins, but none is a controlled test of this exact rule.

entries.claim: AppFollow states that the first three screenshots carry roughly 70% of the conversion weight.
entries.appliesWhen: AppFollow's own claim, attributed to a review of 1,200 top-grossing iOS apps; no data shown.

support.excerpt: AppFollow: 'The first three frames carry roughly 70% of the conversion weight' (Yaroslav Rudnitskiy, reviewing 1,200 top-grossing iOS apps).

entries.useFor: Do not cite as evidence.
entries.researcherNote: Unsourced, unverifiable; listed so the report agent does not reuse it as fact.

entries.claim: About 63% of top game listings use landscape screenshots, against about 5% of non-game listings.
entries.appliesWhen: Observation of top-listed games vs non-games; sample, date and store are not stated (Phiture 2026; Udonis attributes it to Storemaven).

support.excerpt: Phiture: 63% of top gaming apps use landscape-oriented screenshots, compared to just 5% of non-gaming apps.
Udonis: '63% of mobile games use landscape orientation', citing Storemaven.

entries.useFor: Describes the convention Rogue Legend would follow or deliberately break; not evidence of conversion.
entries.researcherNote: Both pages repeat one unsourced statistic; counted as one origin. Says what is common, not what converts.

entries.claim: Screenshot orientation for a game has no proven universal winner, so it is a test variable.
entries.appliesWhen: Games on either store; evidence is one Rovio test plus vendor advice.

support.excerpt: Rovio's SplitMetrics test: portrait screenshots beat landscape for Angry Birds 2 'against industry standards'; earlier landscape gameplay tests had won.
Apple's PPO talk lists screenshot reordering and orientation (landscape vs portrait) among common test themes.
GameAnalytics: A/B test orientation, because 'what works for other games might be toxic for yours'.

counterSupport.excerpt: AppFollow: landscape layouts excel in gaming and streaming where immersion matters more, portrait for utility/finance.

entries.useFor: Plan an orientation test for Rogue Legend rather than assuming; check what the five competitors do first.
entries.researcherNote: No orientation test on Google Play was found. Apple guidance and Rovio are App Store.

entries.claim: On the App Store, landscape screenshot sets were scrolled through to the end more often than portrait sets.
entries.appliesWhen: SplitMetrics 2018, 1,800 tests, 5-image sets; games not isolated.

support.excerpt: SplitMetrics 2018: landscape sets 15% scroll through all 5, portrait 11%; full scrollers convert about 18% (landscape) vs 13% (portrait).

counterSupport.excerpt: AppAgent 2017 found the opposite: 9% scroll portrait sets and 5% landscape.

entries.useFor: Only a hint that landscape can hold attention longer; do not rely on it.
entries.researcherNote: Directly contradicted by AppAgent 2017; both old and iOS-based.

entries.claim: On the App Store, portrait screenshot sets were scrolled through more often than landscape sets, and gamers scrolled more than other users.
entries.appliesWhen: AppAgent 2017: five apps, 25,000+ visitors, three A/B tools.

support.excerpt: AppAgent: 'only 9% of people scroll portrait screenshots', 17% for gamers, 'the scroll rate drops down to 5%' for landscape.
AppsFlyer repeats the 9% / 17% figures citing the Phiture 2017 article.

counterSupport.excerpt: SplitMetrics 2018: 15% landscape vs 11% portrait scroll through all five.

entries.useFor: Shows that scroll-depth evidence on orientation is contradictory; treat as unresolved.
entries.researcherNote: Tiny portfolio sample; AppsFlyer is a relay of the same origin.

entries.claim: A casual audience that holds the phone in portrait can respond better to portrait screenshots than to landscape gameplay screenshots.
entries.appliesWhen: One test (Angry Birds 2, App Store, 99.7% confidence); the audience explanation is the vendor's, not tested.

support.excerpt: SplitMetrics/Rovio: portrait won 'with 99.7% confidence'; conclusion was that a casual audience holding the phone in portrait benefits from portrait screenshots.

counterSupport.excerpt: SplitMetrics 2018 blog reports ZiMAD 'landscape variations' improved conversion 18.4% (details not given).

entries.useFor: Rogue Legend is an idle/roguelike with portrait play; a portrait-vs-landscape test is worthwhile.
entries.researcherNote: Single case; the same vendor reports a landscape win for another game.

entries.claim: A banner-like landscape first screenshot is a pattern to test for games; Social Point reports 15.4% conversion for Monster Legends against 4.7% for a competitor.

facts.of: Monster Legends banner-like landscape first screenshot

entries.appliesWhen: Uncontrolled comparison (own asset vs competitor) reported by GameAnalytics without origin.

support.excerpt: GameAnalytics: Social Point's banner-like landscape first screenshot converted at 15.4% versus 4.7% for its closest competitor.

entries.useFor: Idea for a test variant only.
entries.researcherNote: Not an A/B test; store/date/market unknown; origin unknown.

entries.claim: Screenshots for a game should show the real core loop rather than polished illustrations or menus.
entries.appliesWhen: Games; advice from several vendors, backed by Google's requirement that screenshots show the actual in-game experience.

support.excerpt: Phiture: showcase actual gameplay in screenshots rather than illustrations.
AppFollow audit: 'Go through your own tutorial and use the core loop as the storyboard.'
AppAgent: lead with visual gameplay rather than interface elements (Pocket Paws example).
Google: screenshots must show 'the actual in-app or in-game experience'; not a conversion finding.

counterSupport.excerpt: Udonis: Playrix uses 'artistic interpretations' of gameplay instead of actual screenshots for Homescapes, Gardenscapes and Fishdom.
ZiMAD's +32% redesign replaced plain screenshots with a mix of art overlays and gameplay.

entries.useFor: Base Rogue Legend screenshots on real combat/build frames, dressed with overlays.
entries.researcherNote: No controlled test isolates real gameplay vs art. Google's rule makes pure art non-compliant on Play.

entries.claim: Screenshots that overlay the main character and art on gameplay with action captions beat plain gameplay screenshots in one game test (+32%).
entries.appliesWhen: ZiMAD Bubble Birds 4, iOS implied, duration and sample undisclosed; changes were bundled.

support.excerpt: SplitMetrics: main character overlaid, captions rewritten, plain screenshots replaced with art overlays; '32% more users clicked the install button'.

entries.useFor: Template for a Rogue Legend variant: hero in front, real fight behind, one action caption.
entries.researcherNote: Vendor case study, bundled changes (character, captions, art), no sample/duration. Also see the ab_case entry.

entries.claim: The core mechanic and key text in screenshots must remain legible at thumbnail size.
entries.appliesWhen: Listings viewed on phones and in search lists.

support.excerpt: AppFollow audit: 'Screenshots have to work at thumbnail size'; A Maze Go's maze visuals disappear when reduced.
To ensure your store listing looks great on multiple screen sizes, design for scale and keep important elements toward the center of graphics.
Apple: keep the icon simple and avoid unnecessary detail so it is legible at all sizes.

entries.useFor: Run a thumbnail (squint) check on every Rogue Legend screenshot.
entries.researcherNote: Advice from two audited games plus official guidance; no measured conversion effect.

entries.claim: An AppFollow expert advises zooming in on the mechanic even if the frame no longer looks like the real HUD.
entries.appliesWhen: Single expert opinion from a live audit; may conflict with Google's 'actual experience' rule if taken too far.

support.excerpt: AppFollow audit: 'Zoom in on the mechanic even if it stops looking like the real game HUD.'

entries.useFor: Permission to crop and enlarge the fight/build moment, not to fake it.
entries.researcherNote: One opinion; keep within Google's rule that screenshots reflect the actual in-game experience.

entries.claim: Do not open a game gallery with a menu or inventory screen; open with the experience.
entries.appliesWhen: RPG / midcore listings; vendor advice only.

support.excerpt: ASOMobile: screenshots that open with UI rather than experience are a common mistake; 'the first screenshot isn't the place for an inventory screen'.
AppAgent: lead with a hook, then gameplay, then a reward moment.
AppFollow: lead with gameplay moments, not menus ('Show the dragon battle... Show the reward moment').

entries.useFor: Rogue Legend screenshot 1: combat or boss, not the equipment screen.
entries.researcherNote: Three vendors, no test. Origin count is honest but all are advice.

entries.claim: Each screenshot in the sequence should answer a different question (promise, use case, proof) instead of repeating the same view.
entries.appliesWhen: Advice; no test.

support.excerpt: AppFollow: frame 1 promise, frames 2-3 use cases or outcomes, later frames add proof.
ASOMobile: each screenshot should answer a different player question.

entries.useFor: Structure the 8-slot Play deck as a story: fight, build, progression, reward.
entries.researcherNote: Vendor advice only.

entries.claim: In Homa Games' three-variant screenshot test for Investment Run, the sequence highlighting choices tied to character progression won.
entries.appliesWhen: Publisher's account; no figures, sample or duration; store not stated.

support.excerpt: GameAnalytics/Homa: the third variation 'was the winning bet', showing choices appeal when 'associated with character progression'.

entries.useFor: Supports testing a progression-focused sequence for Rogue Legend.
entries.researcherNote: Qualitative only.

entries.claim: Adding the game's familiar characters to screenshots raised conversion in a game test.
entries.appliesWhen: Rovio Angry Birds 2 (App Store); ZiMAD Bubble Birds 4 bundled a character overlay; Survivor.io shows one foreground character per screenshot (observation).

support.excerpt: SplitMetrics/Rovio: 'familiar characters of the game increased the conversion rate' (no separate confidence figure).
Apptamin (observational): Survivor.io screenshots each show one character in front with colour-coded CTAs.

entries.useFor: Test a hero-forward first screenshot for Rogue Legend versus a gameplay-only one.
entries.researcherNote: The SplitMetrics evidence is one origin; the Survivor.io point is a description, not a test. Familiar IP characters may not transfer to a new IP like Rogue Legend.

entries.claim: Character-led icons beat the original icon in several game icon tests.
entries.appliesWhen: MyTona Seekers Notes (App Store), Homa Investment Run, Frenzoo (Google Play, 2016); one Apple test had a robot character lose.

support.excerpt: SplitMetrics/MyTona: pumpkin-head and smiling-witch icons beat the closed-mouth man control by about 9%.
Homa: for Investment Run 'all the variations featured characters and all of them performed better than the initial listing'.
Frenzoo: an icon with a single avatar over a gameplay background outperformed the original 'with a high degree of confidence' on Google Play.

counterSupport.excerpt: Apple PPO talk: in the Peak Brain Training icon test the robot-character icon performed worse than the control; a brain icon won.

entries.useFor: Include a hero-character icon variant in the first Rogue Legend icon test.
entries.researcherNote: Three origins are game cases, but none discloses samples; Apple's example shows character icons can lose.

entries.claim: In one icon test, characters with an open or smiling mouth beat a closed-mouth character control.
entries.appliesWhen: MyTona Seekers Notes, App Store, undisclosed sample; the 'action mouth' explanation is the vendor's.

support.excerpt: SplitMetrics: 'pumpkin head did 9,3% better than the control'; the witch showed 9.1% growth; all 'action mouth' variants beat the closed-mouth control.

entries.useFor: Weak hint for expressive faces; test rather than assume.
entries.researcherNote: One case; a Halloween theme and a change of character were confounded with the face.

entries.claim: Game icons should be simple, recognisable and distinct from competitors' icons in the same search results.
entries.appliesWhen: Icon design for a store where the icon appears in lists; advice.

support.excerpt: Phiture: 'Your icon needs to be simple, recognizable, and distinct from what competitors are using.'
Apple: create an icon that is simple and recognizable; avoid unnecessary visual details.
AppFollow audit: an icon must differentiate from other icons in the same results set.

entries.useFor: Check Rogue Legend's icon against the five competitors' icons side by side.
entries.researcherNote: Convergent advice; the survivor-like and idle-RPG categories share many similar hero icons, so distinctiveness matters.

entries.claim: Icons with simple, uncluttered backgrounds increased conversion by more than 26% across categories in SplitMetrics 2024 data.
entries.appliesWhen: SplitMetrics 2024 sample of about 200 apps / 3,500+ tests; its published landing page names finance, shopping and utilities, so games are not confirmed.

support.excerpt: AppFollow, quoting SplitMetrics 2024: uncluttered icon backgrounds produced 'conversion increases above 26%'.
SplitMetrics landing page: report data come from 3,500+ tests and cover Finance, Shopping and Utilities (games not named).

entries.useFor: Do not assume the 26% for games.
entries.researcherNote: Second-hand, gated report, category mix probably non-game.

entries.claim: A dark icon can read as a dark smudge on real devices and in dark mode.
entries.appliesWhen: AppFollow audit of an idle/simulation game icon.

support.excerpt: AppFollow audit: on a couple of real devices the dark icon 'reads as a dark smudge'; in dark mode it 'dissolves into the interface'.

entries.useFor: Check Rogue Legend's icon on light and dark home screens.
entries.researcherNote: One audited game; opinion.

entries.claim: Icon tests are among the highest-impact tests for games: Kongregate's icon change gained 92% more installs against 14% for screenshots.
entries.appliesWhen: Google Play (Kongregate Global Assault 2015), Lion Studios 2024 (icons drove the win), SplitMetrics 2024 (icon up to 25% more users, mixed categories).

support.excerpt: Google blog: Kongregate 'found a new icon that drove 92 percent more installs'; variant screenshots gave 14 percent; lesson: start with the icon.
Phiture/Lion Studios: icon tests (+12% then +8%) drove the 20% global install lift for Found It! on Google Play.
SplitMetrics 2024 via AppFollow: icon optimisation can deliver 'up to 25% more users'.

entries.useFor: Put an icon test before a screenshot test in the Rogue Legend roadmap.
entries.researcherNote: Selected successes from vendors; three origins but all vendor-type (no independent data).

entries.claim: A video can raise or lower conversion, so it must be tested against a screenshots-only listing.
entries.appliesWhen: Both stores; evidence mixes iOS and unspecified stores, and apps and games.

support.excerpt: Apple PPO talk: Simply Piano's screenshot treatment beat its app preview by 3.3% at 100% confidence over 12 days.
Storemaven: 'Video can either increase or decrease your conversion rates by 25% and up'.
AppTweak: Expedia and Headway (Jan/Feb 2020) removed their video after A/B tests (no numbers).
Missbeez removed an under-performing video as part of a redesign (+36% page-view-to-install; bundled).

entries.useFor: Rogue Legend should A/B its Play video against no-video or against a different opening.
entries.researcherNote: Non-game examples except where noted; the sole game-type signal is Incipia's correlation.

entries.claim: Among the top 100 free App Store apps, games with a preview video ranked better on average than games without (47 vs 57).

facts.context: Incipia, top 100 free US App Store apps

entries.appliesWhen: Incipia Nov 2023, App Store top 100, correlation only, small subsamples; non-games showed the reverse (62 with vs 46 without).

support.excerpt: Incipia: games with videos averaged rank 47, without 57; non-games with videos 62, without 46.

entries.useFor: Weak support for producing a video at all.
entries.researcherNote: Correlation; popular games may simply afford videos.

entries.claim: A game video should show real gameplay early: within the first 2-10 seconds.
entries.appliesWhen: Play (first 10 seconds, at least 80% representative footage), App Store (first few seconds), vendors (2-3 seconds).

support.excerpt: Show the actual in-app or in-game experience, focusing on the core features and content as early as possible within the first 10 seconds of the video.
Apple: autoplay is muted, so 'make sure the first few seconds of your video are visually compelling'; show more gameplay than cutscenes.
AppAgent: open with gameplay in the first two or three seconds.
AppFollow 2026: the first three seconds carry disproportionate weight.

entries.useFor: Rogue Legend trailer: first frame is a fight, no logo sting.
entries.researcherNote: Google's statement is guidance; vendor timings are assertions.

entries.claim: Videos should be readable with the sound off.
entries.appliesWhen: App Store previews play muted by default; Play inline autoplay is muted.

support.excerpt: Apple: 'By default, app previews play with the sound muted'; text should be legible and stay on screen long enough.
AppAgent: assume the sound is off; the story has to be readable on mute.

entries.useFor: Add on-screen text to the Rogue Legend trailer.
entries.researcherNote: Design guidance.

entries.claim: Google Play documents that the first 30 seconds of a promo video autoplay, so do not assume Play visitors must tap play.
entries.appliesWhen: Play product page as documented by Google (muted inline autoplay); AppFollow 2026 says Play autoplay occurs on the product page but not in search.

support.excerpt: only the first 30 seconds autoplays
AppFollow 2026: Google Play 'product page autoplay behavior only' (not search); iOS partial autoplay on search and product page.

counterSupport.excerpt: Apptamin (undated): on the Play Store videos require the user to tap play, unlike iOS autoplay.

entries.useFor: Treat the first seconds of the Play video as seen by many visitors; verify in Play Console acquisition data.
entries.researcherNote: Older vendor material says the opposite; Google's own page is the newest authority. Behaviour may differ by device and user setting.

entries.claim: Only about 6% of Google Play visitors play the promo video (Storemaven, older data).
entries.appliesWhen: Storemaven claim from before Google's documented autoplay; only known from search-result summaries, not a fetched page.

support.excerpt: Search-result summary of Storemaven: on Google Play videos are not autoplay, so only about 6% of visitors play the video.

entries.useFor: Do not use.
entries.researcherNote: Unfetchable source; probably outdated.

entries.claim: About 10% of viewers stop watching every 5 seconds of a store video.
entries.appliesWhen: Storemaven estimate relayed by Apptamin; unspecified store and date.

support.excerpt: Apptamin: 'Storemaven estimates that an average of 10% of viewers discontinue watching every 5 seconds'.
Apptamin 2018: '10% of them drop every 5 seconds'.

entries.useFor: Front-load the trailer.
entries.researcherNote: Both pages repeat one Storemaven figure (one origin).

entries.claim: The video poster frame or thumbnail is a high-leverage image that should be chosen deliberately.
entries.appliesWhen: Apple poster frames show when autoplay is off; on Play the YouTube thumbnail is picked at random unless set; Kabam +66% relayed second-hand.

support.excerpt: Apple: 'Select a visually compelling poster frame from your footage that conveys the essence of your app'.
AppFollow: with a portrait video, YouTube picks a random frame for the thumbnail unless you choose one.
Incipia relaying Storemaven: testing the Marvel Contest of Champions poster frame gave a 66% conversion increase.

entries.useFor: Set the YouTube thumbnail manually and test it.
entries.researcherNote: Kabam figure is a vendor anecdote (no sample), App Store.

entries.claim: Google's portrait video format showed 7% more watch time and 5% better conversion in early tests, as reported by AppTweak.
entries.appliesWhen: Google I/O 2025 coverage by AppTweak, relayed by Phiture; Google primary not seen.

support.excerpt: Phiture: portrait video showed '7% more watch time, 5% better conversion' (source: AppTweak's Google I/O 2025 coverage).

counterSupport.excerpt: AppFollow: a portrait video upload removes the feature graphic on Google Play.

entries.useFor: Consider a portrait trailer test for Rogue Legend on Play.
entries.researcherNote: Second-hand; scope of the test unknown; uploading portrait video has a side-effect on the feature graphic.

entries.claim: On Google Play the feature graphic is the cover for the promo video and is shown large for games, and it appeared on the listing only when a promo video existed (as of 2023).
entries.appliesWhen: Play listing layout, subject to Google changes; Apptamin observation Jan 2023.

support.excerpt: Google: the feature graphic is a 'cover image for your preview video, if present' and, for games, is shown in a large format alongside preview videos and screenshots.
Apptamin (Jan 2023): 'If you do not have a promo video, the feature graphic will not be displayed on your listing.'

entries.useFor: Plan the feature graphic and the video together.
entries.researcherNote: Layout may have changed since 2023; verify on a current device.

entries.claim: Feature graphics should use vibrant colours, avoid pure white or dark grey, keep the focal point central and keep copy short and large.
entries.appliesWhen: Google Play feature graphic (1024x500); guidance, no conversion data.

support.excerpt: Google: use more vibrant colours, avoid pure white or dark grey (they blend into the Play background), keep the focal point toward the centre.
Apptamin: keep copy short and large; avoid important text near the edges; position visuals around the play-button overlay.

entries.useFor: Use as a checklist for the Rogue Legend feature graphic.
entries.researcherNote: No published conversion test for feature graphics in games was found.

entries.claim: Screenshot captions should be very short (roughly 3-5 words) and large.
entries.appliesWhen: Advice and one before/after redesign; Google caps tagline area at 20% of the image.

support.excerpt: AppFollow: keep text under five words; design for roughly 60pt or larger on export.
Missbeez redesign used large minimal text of 3-4 words per image (part of a +36% before/after change).
AppTweak: add short, benefit-driven captions.

entries.useFor: One short line per Rogue Legend screenshot.
entries.researcherNote: No isolated test on length; the Missbeez result is bundled and the app is not a game.

entries.claim: Benefit, action or use-case captions are recommended over feature labels, but no isolated test of caption wording was found.
entries.appliesWhen: ZiMAD bundled action captions with other changes; Incipia is a rank correlation on the App Store.

support.excerpt: ZiMAD's winning redesign also rewrote captions ('Birds challenge you!' instead of 'Challenging and rewarding gameplay').
Incipia: use-case captions averaged rank 11.8, feature descriptions 48, step-by-step 57, sales/branding 61.
AppTweak recommends benefit-driven captions (no data).

entries.useFor: Write Rogue Legend captions as player outcomes; test two wordings.
entries.researcherNote: Bundled and correlational evidence; the build may label this as multi-origin, but no source isolates wording.

entries.claim: A calmer gradient screenshot background beat an eye-catching background template by 31% in one App Store test.
entries.appliesWhen: Empire City Casino (social casino), 98.6% confidence, duration and sample not stated.

support.excerpt: SplitMetrics: the calmer gradient variant produced '+31% more installs' at 98.6% confidence.

counterSupport.excerpt: ZiMAD's Japan test favoured a dense, effect-heavy Japanese-style set (+36%).

entries.useFor: Test a low-clutter variant against Rogue Legend's busy baseline, especially outside Japan.
entries.researcherNote: Single case; conflicts with the Japan-style dense set, suggesting market dependence.

entries.claim: Vibrant, high-contrast colour is recommended for store graphics, but its effect size for games is not measured in the sources found.
entries.appliesWhen: Feature-graphic guidance (Google) and vendor assertions.

support.excerpt: Google: use more vibrant colours in the feature graphic and avoid pure white or dark grey.
AppTweak asserts that bright, high-contrast designs convert better (no data cited).

entries.useFor: Do not cite a number.
entries.researcherNote: No experiment found.

entries.claim: Text overlays and taglines should be localised for each market, while the in-game UI itself does not need to be.
entries.appliesWhen: Google Play listings with text on screenshots or in videos.

support.excerpt: In-game UI does not need to be localized per market, but any additional taglines or text overlays should be localized.
For screenshots that contain text, provide separate screenshots and promotional videos for each language that you support.
App Radar (PocketGamer.biz): localise screenshots for target audiences, including cultural adaptation.

entries.useFor: Build separate Rogue Legend caption layers for JP, KR, TW/HK (traditional Chinese), TH, VN, ID, PH.
entries.researcherNote: Google guidance, not a conversion finding.

entries.claim: Adapting screenshot style to a market (not only translating captions) can beat one global set: ZiMAD's Japanese-style set gained 36%.
entries.appliesWhen: One App Store test in Japan (game unnamed on the page); advisors recommend cultural adaptation.

support.excerpt: SplitMetrics: optimising screenshots for Japan 'resulted in 36% conversion rate increase'; the winner had lots of small elements and special effects.
AppTweak: Japanese store screenshots are more crowded with more text than Western ones.

entries.useFor: Build a Japan-specific Rogue Legend set and test it against the global set.
entries.researcherNote: Single test; no duration or sample; not Google Play.

entries.claim: Screenshots in Japan tend to carry more text and be more crowded than Western ones.
entries.appliesWhen: Observation of live Japanese product pages (AppTweak advice; SplitMetrics analysis of listings); App Store centred.

support.excerpt: AppTweak: 'Screenshots in the Japanese app stores tend to have more text and to be more crowded than in the West'.
SplitMetrics (2024): apps in Japan 'aren't shy about using space more efficiently', showing offers, reviews and other details.

entries.useFor: Do not copy Western minimalism to Japan without a test.
entries.researcherNote: Observational and advisory; no controlled test other than ZiMAD (single).

entries.claim: Japanese game listings put anime or manga characters and mascots in the foreground.
entries.appliesWhen: Observational advice for games in Japan.

support.excerpt: AppTweak: 'For games, add anime or manga characters in the foreground to highlight them'.
SplitMetrics: mascots are used extensively on Japanese product pages (bunnies, puppies, pillows).

entries.useFor: Test a character-forward Japan variant.
entries.researcherNote: No measured effect.

entries.claim: Japanese App Store listings commonly show 'No. 1' ranking badges on the first screenshot, which Google Play does not allow in images.
entries.appliesWhen: SplitMetrics observation of the Japanese App Store; Google metadata policy bars ranking images on Play.

support.excerpt: SplitMetrics: 'No. 1' badges are prominently displayed on first screenshots across categories in Japan (observational).
Images or text that indicate store performance or ranking, such as 'App of the year,' '#1,' 'Best of Play 20XX,'

entries.useFor: Do not copy the badge onto Play creatives; use it only for App Store JP.
entries.researcherNote: Observation only; the Google line is an excerpt of the policy list.

entries.claim: AppTweak says Koreans prefer complex, anime-style creatives over minimalist Western design, but another ASO author disputes this.
entries.appliesWhen: Korea; opinion only.

support.excerpt: seoasoorm quoting AppTweak: Koreans prefer 'complex and anime creatives rather than the minimalist and realistic design found in the West'.

counterSupport.excerpt: seoasoorm's author disagrees: popular Korean apps use simple, clean, minimalist designs with one-colour palettes.

entries.useFor: Test both a dense and a clean set for KR rather than assuming.
entries.researcherNote: Contested opinion with no test data on either side.

entries.claim: Seasonal or festive store creative can beat the standard version: MyTona's Halloween icons won by about 9%, and SplitMetrics is quoted as finding a 47% festive-icon uplift.
entries.appliesWhen: App Store icon tests; the 47% figure is second-hand without test details.

support.excerpt: SplitMetrics/MyTona Halloween icon variants each beat the control (pumpkin +9.3%, witch +9.1%).
Phiture quoting SplitMetrics: incorporating festive elements into an app icon delivered a 47% conversion uplift.

counterSupport.excerpt: Apple PPO talk: Angry Birds 2's evergreen creative beat holiday-themed creative by 1.5% over 20 days.

entries.useFor: Test seasonal variants; keep the evergreen control.
entries.researcherNote: Both SplitMetrics: one origin. Apple's Angry Birds test points the other way.

entries.claim: For Angry Birds 2 in December, evergreen creative beat holiday-themed creative by 1.5%.
entries.appliesWhen: Apple PPO example: 20 days, about 2 million impressions per treatment, App Store.

support.excerpt: Apple PPO talk: the evergreen control outperformed the holiday-themed content by 1.5% with 100% confidence.

entries.useFor: Do not assume seasonal wins; small effect, large sample.
entries.researcherNote: Apple example; result is specific to this game and creative.

entries.claim: Avoid time-sensitive taglines and seasonal references in screenshots and videos.
entries.appliesWhen: Google screenshot/tagline guidance and Apple app-preview guidance; not an enforced rule in the extracts read.

support.excerpt: Avoid time-sensitive tagline or content that can become outdated quickly to reduce the need to update.
Avoid any seasonal or timely references that will age your video, such as 'new for spring' or dates

entries.useFor: Keep evergreen main sets; run seasonal tests as time-boxed variants or custom listings.
entries.researcherNote: Guidance to limit update work, in tension with seasonal test wins above.

entries.claim: Screenshots that showcase live events or tournaments converting better than regular gameplay is an untested hypothesis.
entries.appliesWhen: Udonis guide; no data.

support.excerpt: Udonis suggests testing the hypothesis that screenshots showing live events and tournaments convert better than regular gameplay; no supporting data given.

entries.useFor: Candidate A/B test theme for event-driven roguelike/idle games.
entries.researcherNote: Hypothesis only.

entries.claim: The widely quoted 30% conversion lift for panoramic screenshots has no linked test, and no isolated panoramic test was found.
entries.appliesWhen: Panoramic (continuous) screenshot sets on either store.

support.excerpt: AppScreenshotStudio: tool pages claim a 30% lift from SplitMetrics/Storemaven data but 'link to no specific test, case study, or published number'.
Missbeez (non-game): +36% page-view-to-install after a bundled redesign incl. panoramic images and a removed video.

entries.useFor: Treat panoramic as a style choice to test; keep frame 1 self-sufficient.
entries.researcherNote: Absence of evidence; the vendor debunking it sells screenshot tooling.

entries.claim: Reordering existing screenshots is a cheap test that has produced lifts between about 6% and 26% in game cases.
entries.appliesWhen: App Store: SEGA +25.6% and ZiMAD (SplitMetrics 2018), ŠKODA LittleDriver +15% (SplitMetrics) or +6.4% (Sensor Tower post); details and dates largely missing.

support.excerpt: SplitMetrics/ŠKODA LittleDriver: reordered existing screenshots improved conversion by 15% and took five minutes to set up.
SplitMetrics 2018 blog: SEGA achieved a 25.6% conversion increase through reordering (details not given).
Sensor Tower post (July 2015): reordered ŠKODA screenshots gave a 6.4% increase in installs over 30 days with 1,200+ visitors.

entries.useFor: Cheap first test: reorder the current Rogue Legend set.
entries.researcherNote: The two ŠKODA reports disagree (+15% vs +6.4%); cases are cherry-picked vendor stories from 2015-2018.

entries.claim: In the top 100 free App Store apps, sets of three screenshots or fewer ranked much worse on average than five-screenshot sets.
entries.appliesWhen: Incipia Nov 2023 correlation; 78 of 100 apps used five screenshots; Google requires at least three screenshots for games and allows up to eight.

support.excerpt: Incipia: 78 apps used five screenshots (avg rank 47), 13 used four (58), 6 used three (80), 3 used two (60).

entries.useFor: Do not ship fewer than the full Play deck; do not read as causal.
entries.researcherNote: Correlation, small groups, App Store, apps and games mixed.

entries.claim: Run store listing tests for at least 7 days in whole-week blocks.
entries.appliesWhen: Google Play experiments and Apple PPO.

support.excerpt: Apple: run tests at least one week, in seven-day increments, to cover weekly traffic patterns.
Phiture: run tests long enough, at least 7 days.
MobileAction: Google recommends at least seven days, capturing weekdays and weekends.
Apptamin: make the experiment last at least a full week.
AppFollow: 14 days is the working window for most games; 7 days minimum.

entries.useFor: Default minimum duration for Rogue Legend tests; more for small lifts.
entries.researcherNote: Common baseline across Apple and several vendors.

entries.claim: Small expected lifts need many more visitors and more days than large ones.
entries.appliesWhen: Google Play experiments; illustrated with Apple examples of 154k to 2M impressions per treatment.

support.excerpt: Phiture: a test with more than two variants and a small MDE extends the duration even more.
Apptamin: 'thousands of installs for each version' needed; example calculator result of 19,907 visitors per variant.
Apple examples ran 12-44 days with 154k-2M impressions per treatment.

entries.useFor: Check expected traffic before choosing a variant count.
entries.researcherNote: Illustrative numbers, not benchmarks.

entries.claim: Google Play A/B/B tests (two identical variants) give more control over false positives than plain A/B tests.
entries.appliesWhen: Google Play experiments.

support.excerpt: Phiture: 'A/B/B tests provide more control over the false positive and false negative results'.

entries.useFor: Use A/B/B for high-stakes Play tests.
entries.researcherNote: Single vendor.

entries.claim: A variant that wins by only about 1-2% should not be shipped on that basis.
entries.appliesWhen: SplitMetrics/ZiMAD lesson; vendor advice.

support.excerpt: SplitMetrics/ZiMAD: if a variation wins by 1% or less, don't upload it; 'only the advantage of at least 2%' results in conversion changes in the stores.

entries.useFor: Set a minimum effect threshold before launch.
entries.researcherNote: Single vendor rule of thumb.

entries.claim: Most store experiments should be expected to produce no significant winner; one automated programme found 7 significant wins in 168 experiments.

facts.context: Wildlife Studios; ratio computed here about 4% of experiments

entries.appliesWhen: Wildlife Studios via PressPlay (322 variants, under two months); SplitMetrics explains no-winner outcomes without giving a rate.

support.excerpt: Phiture: 168 experiments, 322 variants, 7 significant wins, max +24.1% conversion, under two months.
SplitMetrics: tests can end with no winner if significance is not reached before the time limit; no frequency is given.

entries.useFor: Budget for many tests; do not promise a win per test.
entries.researcherNote: No published aggregate win rate for game store tests was found; general A/B win rates come from unrelated fields. Wildlife's tests were GenAI-generated assets.

entries.claim: AppFollow's planning defaults for detectable lifts in game tests are 5-10% for first-screenshot hook, icon character and feature graphic, 8-15% for video and 4-8% for screenshot order.

facts.of: first-screenshot hook / icon character / feature graphic

entries.appliesWhen: AppFollow's own table; not measured data.

support.excerpt: AppFollow MDE table: icon character 5-10%, first-screenshot hook 5-10%, video 8-15%, feature graphic 5-10%, screenshot order 4-8%.

entries.useFor: Use as inputs to sample-size planning only.
entries.researcherNote: Planning defaults, not evidence of effects.

entries.claim: About half of top Google Play games ran two or more screenshot A/B tests in a year (51% in 2025; 57% reported for 2024).

facts.of: ran 2+ screenshot tests on Google Play

entries.appliesWhen: AppTweak data on the top 1,000 US apps/games; the 57% is AppTweak's earlier-year figure as relayed by Phiture.

support.excerpt: AppTweak 2026 report: '42% of top apps and 51% of top games ran two or more screenshot tests' on Google Play in 2025.
Phiture (citing AppTweak 2025 benchmark data): 57% of top games on Google Play A/B tested screenshots at least twice that year.

entries.useFor: Benchmark: competitors likely refresh creatives a few times a year.
entries.researcherNote: Same origin (AppTweak) for both years; Phiture's year label is ambiguous. Correlates activity, not effect.

entries.claim: Average 2025 US conversion rate was 16.15% on Google Play against 8.56% on the App Store, and Games-Strategy had the lowest Google Play category rate at 6.6%.
entries.appliesWhen: AppTweak US data; methodology and sample not described; RPG/idle categories not reported.

support.excerpt: AppTweak: in 2025 the US average conversion rate was 8.56% on the App Store and 16.15% on Google Play; Games-Strategy the lowest Google Play category at 6.6%.

entries.useFor: Sanity check for Rogue Legend's Play conversion; not an Asian-market benchmark.
entries.researcherNote: No sample description; roguelike/RPG/idle rates not given; US only.

entries.claim: Custom store listings can lift conversion for targeted traffic: a median 10% in Google Ads campaigns (AppTweak via Phiture) and 15% more installs in Koo's case.

facts.of: custom store listings in Google Ads campaigns
facts.context: AppTweak Google I/O 2025 reporting via Phiture

entries.appliesWhen: Google Play custom store listings; the Koo case is India-based and not a game.

support.excerpt: Phiture: custom store listings show a 'median 10% conversion lift when used in Google Ad campaigns' (source: AppTweak).
Google Play case study index: 'Koo: Custom store listings increase installs 15%'.

entries.useFor: Use per-country custom listings for the JP/KR/TW/SEA creative sets.
entries.researcherNote: Second-hand median; Koo page itself not fetched; not a game.
